definition: A data lake is a system or repository of data stored in its natural, raw format, usually object blobs or files.
details: A data lake is usually a single store of data including raw copies of source system data, sensor data, social data etc., and transformed data used for tasks such as reporting, visualization, advanced analytics, and machine learning. A data lake can include structured data from relational databases (rows and columns), semi-structured data (CSV, logs, XML, JSON), unstructured data (emails, documents, PDFs), and binary data (images, audio, video). A data lake can be established on premises (within an organization's data centers) or in the cloud (using cloud services).

explainer.lead: A data lake keeps many kinds of data together, including copies in their original form. This lets an organization preserve source data while also preparing versions for reports, analysis, and machine learning.

tiers.eli5: A data lake is like a big storage room where you keep things just as they arrived instead of sorting everything first. You might store photos, messages, spreadsheets, and sensor readings there. Later, you can tidy up some copies to make a chart, write a report, or teach a computer to find patterns.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use a data lake as a shared repository for raw source copies and transformed datasets, deployed either on premises or in the cloud. Inputs can range from relational rows and CSV or JSON files to documents, images, audio, and video. Design downstream transformations for the reporting, visualization, analytics, or machine-learning tasks that need them while retaining the raw copies.
tiers.paperLevel: Data lake = a repository storing data in its natural or raw format, commonly as object blobs or files, alongside transformed data. Its contents may be structured, semi-structured, unstructured, or binary. The same repository can support reporting, visualization, advanced analytics, and machine learning, with deployment on premises or in the cloud.

explainer.example: A company stores raw sensor readings as files, customer records copied from a relational database, JSON logs, and PDF documents in one cloud data lake. It then transforms some readings and customer records for a report while retaining the original files for later analysis or machine learning.

usedIn.name: Reporting
usedIn.detail: Transformed data in the lake can supply organizational reports.

usedIn.name: Visualization
usedIn.detail: Prepared datasets can be used to build visual views of the stored information.

usedIn.name: Advanced analytics
usedIn.detail: Analysts can work with varied structured, semi-structured, unstructured, and binary data.

usedIn.name: Machine learning
usedIn.detail: Raw and transformed data can provide material for machine-learning tasks.

explainer.intuition: Instead of forcing every incoming item into one tidy structure first, a data lake preserves data as it arrives. Useful, cleaned-up versions can then be created for particular purposes without discarding the originals.
howItWorks: Collect raw copies from source systems, sensors, and social data.
Store them in their natural formats, commonly as object blobs or files.
Keep structured, semi-structured, unstructured, and binary data in the shared repository.
Transform selected data for reporting, visualization, analytics, or machine learning.
Run the repository in an organization's data centers or using cloud services.
explainer.whyItMatters: A data lake preserves original data while making room for prepared versions, so the same repository can serve several kinds of work. It also accommodates formats that do not fit neatly into rows and columns.
misconceptions: A data lake is not limited to unstructured data; it can also hold relational rows, CSV, XML, JSON, logs, and binary files.
It does not necessarily contain only untouched raw data; transformed data used for downstream tasks can be included too.
